title: Enrolling your child in public school
text: Every child living in the United States has the right to a free public education from kindergarten through 12th grade, regardless of their or their parents' immigration status. The Supreme Court decided this in Plyler v. Doe (1982). Schools may not ask about immigration status and may not require a Social Security number to enroll. To register, districts usually ask for proof of the child's age (such as a birth certificate or passport), proof that you live in the district (such as a lease or utility bill), and immunization records. If you are missing a document, the school must still help you enroll, and children experiencing homelessness can enroll right away under the McKinney-Vento Act.

title: Which school will my child attend?
text: In most US school districts, your home address decides your child's assigned public school, sometimes called the neighborhood or zoned school. You can find it by calling the district office or using the school finder on the district website. Many districts also offer choices: magnet schools focus on a subject like science or the arts, and charter schools are free public schools run independently. These often require an application and may use a lottery, with deadlines months before the school year. Private schools charge tuition. All public schools, including charter and magnet schools, are free and must follow the same rights for students.

title: Enrolling during the school year
text: You can enroll your child in public school at any time of the year, not only in August or September. If your family just arrived, contact the district's enrollment or welcome center as soon as you have an address. Schools should enroll children quickly so they don't miss learning time. Bring whatever documents you have, such as school records, report cards, and vaccination records from your home country. If records are missing or in another language, the school will still enroll your child and may use tests or interviews to decide which classes fit best.

title: School records from another country
text: School records from your home country, like report cards, transcripts, and diplomas, help the new school place your child in the right classes. High schools may use them to give credit for courses already completed. Bring originals and copies if you can. You do not always need an official translation; ask the school what they accept. If you have no records, your child can still enroll. The school may give placement tests, and for high school students, ask the counselor how earlier studies can count toward graduation credits.

title: Rights for children without stable housing
text: The federal McKinney-Vento Act protects children whose families lack a fixed, regular place to live. This includes living in a shelter, motel, car, or campground, or sharing housing with others because of losing housing or economic hardship. These children can enroll in school immediately, even without the usual documents like proof of address or school records. They can stay in their school of origin if they move, and the district must provide transportation when that is in the child's best interest. They also qualify for free school meals. Every district has a McKinney-Vento liaison who can help.

title: Preschool, pre-K, and kindergarten
text: Kindergarten is the first year of elementary school, usually for children who are 5 years old by a date set by each state, often around September 1. Some states require kindergarten and others make it optional, but almost all public schools offer it for free. Many states and districts also offer free or low-cost pre-kindergarten (pre-K) for 3- and 4-year-olds, and the federal Head Start program serves young children from families with low incomes. Spaces can be limited, so apply early. Ask your school district about pre-K programs and registration dates.

title: How grade levels work
text: US schools are usually divided into elementary school (kindergarten to grade 5), middle school or junior high (grades 6 to 8), and high school (grades 9 to 12). Some districts also offer free pre-kindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds. Children are placed in a grade mainly by age; the cutoff birthday for kindergarten (often around September 1) is set by each state. Students arriving from another country are generally placed with children their own age, not held back because they are still learning English. High school students earn credits in each class, and they need a set number of credits to graduate with a diploma.

title: The school year and calendar
text: Most US public schools start in August or September and end in May or June, with about 180 school days in many states. There is usually a winter break in late December, a spring break of about one week, and a long summer break. Schools also close on certain holidays and may have early-release days or teacher workdays with no classes for students. Each district publishes its own calendar, usually on its website, so dates differ from place to place. Ask your school for a copy of the calendar and mark the days off school.

title: What a school day looks like
text: A typical school day lasts about six to seven hours, often starting between 7:30 and 9:00 in the morning. Elementary students usually stay with one main teacher most of the day and have recess, a play break outside. Middle and high school students move between classrooms and teachers for different subjects. Students eat lunch at school, either brought from home or bought from the cafeteria. Arriving on time matters: students who come late usually need to check in at the front office. Start and end times differ by school, so ask yours for its schedule.

title: Who's who at school
text: The principal leads the school, and an assistant principal often helps with discipline and daily operations. Teachers lead classes, and in middle and high school your child will have several. The school counselor helps with class schedules, college plans, and personal or emotional problems. The school nurse handles illness, injuries, and medicines during the day. Many schools also have a social worker or psychologist, an English learner teacher, and a family liaison who helps parents. The front office staff answer phones, take absence calls, and are a good first place to ask any question.

title: Report cards and grades
text: Schools send report cards several times a year, often every quarter or trimester. Many middle and high schools use letter grades: A is excellent, B is good, C is average, D is barely passing, and F means failing. Some use percentages, and elementary schools often use numbers like 1 to 4 to show whether a child meets grade-level standards. High school grades are combined into a grade point average (GPA), usually on a 4.0 scale, which colleges look at. Many districts have an online parent portal where you can see grades, missing assignments and attendance at any time; ask the school office how to get a login.

title: State tests and other standardized tests
text: Federal law requires states to test students in reading and math every year from grades 3 to 8 and once in high school, and in science a few times. These state tests show how well students and schools are doing; the results usually come home months later as a score report. English learners also take a yearly English proficiency test to measure progress in English. Some newcomer students may be excused from the reading test in their first year. In high school, students may also take tests like the PSAT, SAT, or ACT for college. Ask the school what each test is used for.

title: Homework and how to help
text: Most US students get homework, and the amount usually grows in higher grades. Homework often counts toward grades, so missing assignments can lower a report card. You can help even if you don't speak English or know the subject: set a regular time and quiet place, ask your child to explain what they learned, and check that work is finished. Reading together in your home language also builds skills. If homework is too hard or takes too long, tell the teacher. Many schools offer free homework help or tutoring before or after school.

title: What public school costs
text: Public school tuition is free from kindergarten through 12th grade. Families are often asked to buy basic supplies like notebooks, pencils, and a backpack, and schools send a supply list before the year starts. Some schools charge small fees for things like field trips, sports, clubs, or yearbooks. If these costs are hard for your family, ask the school about fee waivers or free supplies; many schools, community groups, and back-to-school events give them away. Students should not be kept out of required classes because a family cannot pay a fee.

title: Support for students learning English
text: Public schools must help students who are learning English, called English learners (ELs or ELLs). When you enroll, you will fill out a home language survey. If a language other than English is used at home, the school tests your child's English and, if needed, provides English language development services such as ESL classes or bilingual programs. These services are free. Federal law, including the Civil Rights Act and the Supreme Court case Lau v. Nichols, requires that English learners get real access to their education. Your child can leave the program once they pass an English proficiency test, and you can ask the school to explain the program options.

title: Special education, IEPs and 504 plans
text: If your child has a disability or you think they learn differently, you can ask the school in writing for a free evaluation. Under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), a child who qualifies gets an Individualized Education Program (IEP): a written plan with goals and services such as speech therapy or extra classroom support. A 504 plan, under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, gives accommodations like extra test time to students whose disability affects learning but who may not need specialized instruction. Parents are members of the IEP team, must give consent, and have the right to an interpreter at IEP meetings and to have documents explained in their language.

title: If your child is struggling in school
text: If your child's grades drop, they seem unhappy, or they say school is too hard, contact the teacher first and ask for a meeting. Ask what your child does well, where they struggle, and what help is available. Many schools offer extra support such as small-group lessons, tutoring, or reading and math intervention programs, often at no cost. Keep notes and copies of messages. If the problems continue, you can ask the counselor for help or ask in writing for a special education evaluation. Struggling with English alone is not a disability, but a child can be both learning English and have a disability.

title: Gifted and advanced programs
text: Many districts offer gifted and talented (GT) programs or advanced classes for students who learn quickly or show strong abilities. There is no single national rule, so how students are chosen differs by state and district; it may include tests, grades, and teacher recommendations. English learners can be gifted, and schools should not leave them out just because they are still learning English. In middle and high school, students may take honors or Advanced Placement (AP) classes. If you think your child needs more challenge, ask the teacher or counselor how to request a gifted evaluation.

title: Free tutoring and extra help
text: If your child is learning English, the most important help is the school's English learner program: public schools must test students who speak another language at home and provide free English language services, like ESL classes, to those who need them. Many schools also offer free extra help, such as tutoring before or after school, homework clubs, summer school, or online learning programs. Schools that receive federal Title I funding, which serves many students from families with lower incomes, often have additional support programs. Public libraries usually offer free homework help, computers, and sometimes tutoring in several languages. Community centers and nonprofit organizations may also provide free tutoring. Ask your child's teacher or counselor what is available, and tell them which language your family speaks so they can suggest the best options.

title: Your right to an interpreter
text: Schools must communicate important information to parents in a language they understand. This includes enrollment, report cards, discipline, special education, and parent-teacher conferences. You can ask for a free interpreter or translated documents, and the school should not ask your child or another student to interpret for you. Many schools use apps or email to send news, so tell the office which language you prefer. If the school does not provide language help, you can ask the principal or the district office, and you have the right to file a complaint.

title: Parent-teacher conferences
text: Parent-teacher conferences are short meetings, usually once or twice a year, where the teacher shares how your child is doing in learning and behavior. They often last 15 to 20 minutes, and many schools offer in-person, phone, or video options. You can ask for a free interpreter ahead of time. Good questions to ask include: How is my child doing compared to grade level? What are their strengths? Where do they need help? How can I help at home? You can also ask to meet the teacher at other times during the year, not only at conference time.

title: Student records and privacy (FERPA)
text: A federal law called FERPA gives parents the right to see their child's school records, such as grades, attendance, and discipline files. The school must let you review them within 45 days of your request. You can ask the school to correct information you believe is wrong. In most cases, schools need a parent's written permission before sharing a student's records with others, though there are some exceptions. Schools may share basic directory information, like name and grade, unless you tell them in writing not to. These rights pass to the student at age 18.

title: School discipline and suspensions
text: Every school has a code of conduct that explains its rules and consequences, usually shared at the start of the year. Consequences can include detention, losing privileges, suspension (being kept out of school for some days), or, for serious cases, expulsion. Parents should be told when their child is suspended, and students generally have a right to hear what they are accused of and tell their side. You can ask for a meeting, an interpreter, and the steps to appeal. Students with disabilities have extra protections, including a review if they are removed for more than 10 school days.

title: If you face discrimination at school
text: Federal civil rights laws protect students from discrimination based on race, color, national origin (which includes language), sex, and disability in public schools. This also covers harassment by other students that the school ignores. If you believe your child is treated unfairly, write down what happened, with dates and names, and report it to the principal or the district. You can ask for an interpreter. If the problem is not fixed, you can file a complaint with the US Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights, generally within 180 days of what happened.

title: Immigration status and school
text: Your child's right to attend public school does not depend on their or your immigration status. Schools should not ask about status, and you do not have to share it to enroll. FERPA, the student privacy law, generally requires parent permission before schools share student records, with some exceptions such as a court order. Many families make a safety plan: keep emergency contacts up to date with trusted adults who can pick up your child, and know your rights. Immigration enforcement rules can change, so for questions about your own situation, contact a qualified immigration lawyer or nonprofit legal aid organization.

title: Getting involved at your child's school
text: US schools welcome parent involvement, and you don't need to speak perfect English to take part. Many schools have a parent group, called a PTA or PTO, that holds meetings and events. Some schools have committees for families of English learners. You can volunteer in classrooms, at events, or on field trips; some districts require a background check for volunteers, so ask what ID is accepted. Local school boards hold public meetings where parents can speak. Even simple steps, like reading school messages and attending family nights, help your child succeed.

title: Emergency contacts and pickup
text: When you enroll, the school asks for emergency contacts: trusted adults the school can call if your child is sick, hurt, or if you cannot be reached. Schools only release children to adults listed on their record, so keep this list current and include people who can pick up your child if you can't. Tell the school right away when your phone number or address changes. If there is a custody arrangement or a court order about who may pick up your child, give a copy to the school office so staff know who is allowed.

title: Free and reduced-price school meals
text: Through the National School Lunch Program and School Breakfast Program, children from families with lower incomes can get free or reduced-price meals at school. Eligibility is based on household size and income, not immigration status. You do not need a Social Security number for your child; on the application, the adult filling it out can mark that they do not have one. School meals have not been counted in immigration public charge rules, but rules can change, so ask a nonprofit legal aid organization if you are worried. Some schools offer free meals to every student through the Community Eligibility Provision. Applications are available from the school office or district website and can be submitted at any time during the year.

title: Attendance and absences
text: Every state has compulsory attendance laws that require children to attend school, usually from about age 6 until 16 or 18 depending on the state. When your child is absent, contact the school the same day and give the reason, such as illness or a family emergency; schools may ask for a note. Too many unexcused absences can be considered truancy, which may lead to meetings with the school and, in some states, court involvement. Missing 10 percent or more of the school year, called chronic absenteeism, can hurt learning even if the absences are excused. If something is making it hard for your child to attend, ask the school counselor for help.

title: School buses and getting to school
text: Many districts provide free school buses for students who live farther than a set distance from school; the distance rules differ by district. Ask the school or district transportation office if your child qualifies, where the bus stop is, and the pickup times. Students who live close to school usually walk, bike, or are driven. Children without stable housing may get transportation to their school of origin, and students with disabilities get transportation if their IEP includes it. Teach your child bus safety, and tell the school if your child needs a different stop or a changed schedule.

title: Weather closures and emergencies
text: Schools may close or start late because of snow, storms, extreme heat, or other emergencies. Districts announce closures by text, phone call, email, app notifications, their website, and local TV or radio. Make sure the school has your current phone number and preferred language so you get these messages. Schools also practice safety drills, such as fire drills and lockdown drills, so students know what to do in an emergency. During a real emergency, follow the school's instructions about where to pick up your child rather than going straight to the building.

title: Dress codes and uniforms
text: Most US schools have a dress code that explains what students may not wear, such as clothing with offensive words or very revealing clothes. Some public schools require uniforms, often simple items like polo shirts and plain pants in certain colors. If your school requires uniforms and the cost is hard for your family, ask the school about free or donated uniforms. Students can generally wear religious clothing, such as head coverings, even when a dress code exists. Check the student handbook or ask the office for your school's rules.

title: School technology and the parent portal
text: Many schools give students a laptop or tablet for schoolwork, which may come home each night. Families may be asked to sign an agreement about caring for the device. Teachers often post assignments online, so students may need internet at home; if you don't have internet, ask the school about hotspots or low-cost options, and public libraries offer free Wi-Fi. Most districts also have a parent portal, a website or app where you can see grades, attendance, and messages. Ask the front office for your login and help setting it up in your language.

title: Before- and after-school programs
text: Many schools and community organizations offer before- and after-school programs, where children can stay safely while parents work. These may include homework help, sports, art, and snacks. Some are free, especially programs funded for schools serving families with lower incomes, while others charge fees, sometimes with discounts based on income. Clubs and sports teams also meet after school, mostly in middle and high school. Ask your school's front office or district website what programs exist and how to sign up, since spaces can fill quickly at the start of the year.

title: Field trips and permission slips
text: A field trip is a school outing to a place like a museum, farm, or theater. Before a trip, the school sends home a permission slip, a form a parent signs to allow the child to go. Without a signed form, a child usually cannot attend and stays at school. The form may ask for a small fee or a packed lunch; if cost is a problem, ask the teacher, because schools often have help available. Read forms that come home in your child's backpack, and ask the school to translate them if needed.

title: Vaccines and health requirements
text: Every state requires certain vaccinations, also called immunizations or shots, for school, such as those for measles, polio, and whooping cough. The exact list and the rules for medical or other exemptions differ by state. Bring any vaccination records from your home country; a doctor or clinic can review them and give missing doses. Some states also require a physical exam, vision or hearing screening, or a dental check. The federal Vaccines for Children program provides free vaccines to eligible children, including those without health insurance. Your local health department can tell you where to go.

title: The school nurse and medicines
text: Many schools have a nurse or health office that helps students who feel sick or get hurt during the day and calls parents when needed. If your child needs to take medicine at school, including inhalers for asthma or medicine for allergies, you usually must fill out a form, often signed by a doctor, and bring the medicine in its original labeled container. Tell the school about any health conditions or allergies. Keep your child home if they have a fever or are vomiting, and follow the school's rules for when they can return.

title: Health insurance for children
text: Children in families with low or moderate incomes may qualify for free or low-cost health insurance through Medicaid or CHIP, the Children's Health Insurance Program. Rules for immigrant children differ by state and by immigration situation, and some states cover more children using state funds. A parent can apply for an eligible child without applying for themselves, and parents who are not applying do not have to share their own immigration status. School nurses and community health centers can help you apply. For questions about immigration effects, ask a nonprofit legal aid organization.

title: Bullying
text: Bullying is repeated, unwanted behavior meant to hurt someone, such as hitting, name-calling, spreading rumors, leaving someone out, or harassment online. Signs your child may be bullied include not wanting to go to school, lost belongings, trouble sleeping, or sudden sadness. Listen calmly and write down what happened, when, and who was involved. Report it to the teacher, counselor, or principal, and ask what the school will do and when they will follow up. Schools must respond to bullying, especially harassment based on race, national origin, religion, sex, or disability.

title: Mental health and emotional support
text: Moving to a new country and school can be stressful for children. Signs they may need support include ongoing sadness, anger, withdrawal from friends, changes in sleep or eating, or falling grades. School counselors, psychologists, and social workers can talk with students and connect families with free or low-cost services, and you can ask for help in your language. If your child talks about hurting themselves or is in crisis, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.

title: High school credits and graduation
text: To earn a high school diploma, students must pass a required number of credits in subjects like English, math, science, and social studies, plus electives they choose. A credit usually equals one class passed for a full year; each state and district sets its own requirements, and some states also require exams. Students who fail a required class may need to repeat it or take credit recovery. Meet with the school counselor early, ideally in 9th grade, to review the graduation plan and ask whether courses from another country can count.

title: Preparing for college
text: Preparing for college starts early in high school. Good grades in challenging classes matter, and many students take honors, Advanced Placement (AP), or dual enrollment classes, which can earn college credit while still in high school. Many colleges look at SAT or ACT scores, though some no longer require them. Activities like clubs, sports, volunteering, and jobs also help. Community colleges offer two-year programs at lower cost and can lead to a four-year university. The school counselor can help your child plan courses, find programs, and meet application deadlines, usually in the fall of 12th grade.

title: AP classes and college credit
text: Advanced Placement (AP) courses are college-level classes taught in high school, such as AP Computer Science A, AP Calculus, or AP Biology. Each course ends with an AP Exam in May, scored from 1 to 5. Many colleges give credit, placement into a higher-level class, or both for qualifying scores, often a 3, 4, or 5. Each college sets its own rules, which can differ by subject and change from year to year, so a score that earns credit at one college may not at another. To check a college's policy, use College Board's AP Credit Policy Search or the college's official website, usually on the admissions or registrar page. Students send AP scores to colleges through their College Board account. Students from families with lower incomes may qualify for a reduced exam fee; ask the school's AP coordinator.

title: Paying for college
text: The FAFSA, the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, is how students apply for federal grants, loans, and work-study, and many states and colleges use it too. Students who are US citizens or eligible noncitizens can apply even if their parents do not have a Social Security number; parents can still complete their part. Students without lawful status generally cannot get federal aid, but some states offer in-state tuition or state aid to them, and these rules change. Scholarships from colleges and private groups are another option. Learn more at studentaid.gov or ask the school counselor.

title: Older students and age limits
text: Teenagers who arrive in the US can enroll in public high school. Most states allow students to attend free public school until about age 21, though the exact age limit differs by state. Older newcomers with few credits may find it hard to graduate in time, so some districts offer newcomer programs, international high schools, or extra time. Other options include adult education, high school equivalency programs like the GED, and community college. A counselor can explain which path fits your child's age, credits, and goals.

title: Classes for parents
text: Many school districts, community colleges, and libraries offer free or low-cost classes for adults, including English as a Second Language (ESL), citizenship preparation, computer skills, and high school equivalency programs like the GED. Some schools offer parent workshops on topics like using the parent portal, helping with homework, or planning for college. Learning English can help you talk with teachers, but you have the right to an interpreter even while you are learning. Ask your child's school or your local library about classes for parents.
